items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1965-09-13
items.q: I worked there with a little three-piece group with Chink Morton's son, who played banjo, and Eddie Miller, who played alto sax in those days.

ctx.x: I just want to get one more thing on the biography before we go on. After you started with this group at the Fern, was it? Yeah. Did you do mostly after that single work? I've known you always as a single since I was first a jazz fan. Did you have any other gigs that you think were especially worthy of note, either with a group or as a single, that were important to you as you developed in your career?

Not as a single, Charlie, because I worked with groups there. I went from the Fern dance hall over to a little nightclub or cabaret, they call it in those days, called the Valencia, where the Hilton Inn is supposed to go up today on Bourbon Street. And I worked there with a little three-piece group with Chink Morton's son, who played banjo, and Eddie Miller, who played alto sax in those days. And we had a little three-piece outfit. And, well, from there I went to various places. I don't know if I can get them…

This seems to be something that's always struck me as sort of almost a tradition among New Orleans musicians, the reluctance to leave town. I guess Chicago, almost forced out because of the closing of Storyville, and then we know on the current pop charts, our hurt, you know, for a long time resisted leaving town, and so did Pete Fountain. Have you ever thought about this? Why is that there's such a reluctance on the part of major talents, such as yourself, to leave town? It seems like there are big markets…

items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1960-07-14
items.q: I joined the Owls when they were at the halfway house. That's when Eddie Miller was playing with them.

ctx.x: He played, he played bass on some of the picnics that I played out there with. Uh, Angie Jumeli played on some of them out there. He played Sousa Porn out there. Uh, some of the trumpet players, I think, were Tony Foucherai. And, uh, Red Bowman, trumpet player. Incidentally, speaking of trumpet players, you must forget, uh, Bill Padron. Bill Padron played fine trumpet. I played with him with the Owls Orchestra, you know. I joined the Owls when they were at the halfway house. That's when Eddie Miller was playing…
I don't know that. I don't know that.

items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1976-02-13
items.q: my friend Eddie Miller and Dan LeBlanc was a fine musician. Angelo Palmezana, we were all playing in a band together at the time.

ctx.x: Before, I'm going to ask you to play a few things on the piano. Yeah. Because I think it shows the kind of thing you've been talking about with the piano and the cornet. But could you just relate the meeting with the Whiteman Orchestra at the St. Charles Theater? Yes. And I think it's an interesting story.

Well, I think it was probably one of the most exciting things that I can remember happening in my musical career. I don't know of any, I've had quite a few nice things happen, but this probably had to be one of the most exciting because, as I say, Bix was, well, it was a magic word at that time. And when we found out that Paul Whiteman was going to tour down this way and he was going to be at the St. Charles Theater, which is no longer here now, they tour it now. Why? This was something that everybody just looked…

come out there too. So we went back into the theater and when Mike Whiteman got finished playing Concerto O'NF by Gershwin, he put his baton on and he says, well, he says, all I can say is now, he says, I think I better turn it over to Bix and let him take over. He says, oh, they're going to tear this place down.
